description:
Olá! Sou Felipe Gama, graduando em Engenharia da Computação na FAINOR, com foco em Inteligência Artificial. Tenho habilidades em Python, SQL, análise de dados e desenvolvimento de APIs com FastAPI, além de experiência em projetos com agentes inteligentes.

Tenho interesse em transformar dados em soluções úteis, especialmente em aplicações que conectem tecnologia, sustentabilidade e problemas reais. No hackathon, quero contribuir com o desenvolvimento do protótipo, a integração de dados da NASA.
summary:
Inspot is a mobile app that helps people anywhere check what they hear about the climate of the place where they live. The user writes what they noticed, for example “it is raining less in my city”. The app turns that sentence into a question, looks for the answer in four public datasets with global or near-global coverage (NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, CHIRPS and ERA5) and calculates the trend in each one. The result is a verdict in plain language, such as “probable decrease”, that shows how many sources agree.

Because the data covers the planet, the same method works for any city. We started with three cities in the interior of Bahia, Brazil, where the app showed that temperature has risen in all of them, while the drop in rainfall people talk about is confirmed by only one source.

This addresses the challenge because the app selects the variables, gets regional data, uses long time series and measures the rate of change with a significance test. NASA data is public and global, but hard to use. Our goal is for students and communities in any country to verify things by themselves instead of repeating what they heard.
details:
What it does and how it works

The user starts with an everyday statement. The app identifies the place and the variable, and asks the same question to several datasets. For each dataset we use one value per year and calculate the rate of change per decade (Theil-Sen slope) and its significance (Mann-Kendall test). Then we compare the sources. If two or more confirm the change, there is consensus. If they only point in the same direction, the result is “probable”. If they disagree, the app says so.

We tested it with real data for three cities in Bahia, Brazil, and for twelve points across the region. One example: in Barreiras, one source shows rainfall falling by 42 mm per decade, but the other three do not confirm it. Temperature, on the other hand, rose in all three cities according to both sources we used.

Benefits and impact

In the interior of Bahia, a late or weak rainy season decides what a family plants, how much water a town stores and whether a harvest pays off. People there hear every year that the climate has changed, but they have no way to check it. inspot gives them that way. In a few seconds, anyone can see whether a change is confirmed by several sources, only probable, or not supported by the data at all.

This changes three things. Farmers and local managers can tell a real trend from a bad year before making long-term decisions. Students learn to check a claim with evidence instead of accepting or rejecting it by opinion. And news about the climate can be compared with the record by any reader, which makes exaggeration and denial equally easy to spot.

The impact also reaches NASA. Every question asked and every local report sent shows what people notice on the ground and what they want to know, something satellites cannot measure. Because the datasets cover the planet, the same benefit applies to any city, not only to the ones we tested.

People can understand the result without knowing statistics, and they can see which years were analysed. We also designed a community area for local reports and a field mode where the user photographs what they see.

Learning

inspot is also a place to learn. A detective character guides the student through five short missions, each one built on a real case from the data: why one source is not enough, what a trend is, how to read a line chart, how to check a headline against the record, and how different datasets measure the same thing. In the “climate court”, two AI agents argue for and against a statement using only the calculated numbers, and the student gives the verdict before seeing what the sources say. Every explanation can be read at three levels, from elementary school to university. Students earn badges and a free certificate. We want them to leave knowing how to question a claim about the climate, not only what the answer was.

Tools

Python to download and process the data. HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the prototype. Data: NASA POWER, GPM IMERG and CHIRPS (through ClimateSERV), ERA5 (through Open-Meteo) and NOAA’s ONI index. We used AI assistants such as Claude Code and Codex to support coding and text review. We used Photoshop for the initial asset concepts of the visual identity, and ChatGPT for image generation and video editing.

Creativity

We treat the analysis as an investigation. The user brings the case, the app is the detective and the datasets are the witnesses. Showing when sources disagree, instead of hiding it, is the core of the idea.

What we considered

We do not forecast and we do not assign causes. The verdict is an estimate, not a final answer. We know the sources are not fully independent. Three cities are a start, but the datasets cover the planet, so the same method can be applied anywhere. We have not yet measured the impact with real users; that is the next step.
